ai.text:
The European Parliament has approved a regulation on how courts handle cases involving adults who cannot fully protect their own interests because of an impairment or insufficiency of their personal faculties, when those cases cross national borders in the European Union. The vote was 531 in favour and 93 against, with 41 abstentions. The regulation covers measures such as those listed in the 2000 Hague Convention on the International Protection of Adults, as well as measures that help an adult exercise their legal capacity and powers of representation that an adult has granted to someone else.

Under the rules on choice of court, a court in a Member State other than the adult's place of habitual residence can take protective measures if four conditions are all met. The adult must have chosen that court at a time when they were able to make that choice. At that time, the chosen country must be one of four kinds: the adult's own nationality, the adult's habitual residence, the habitual residence of a close person willing to take on protective responsibility, or a country where the adult owns property. Taking jurisdiction must also not go against the adult's interests, and courts that have jurisdiction under the 2000 Hague Convention must not already have acted. The choice must be in writing, dated and signed, or made electronically in a way that can be durably recorded. Before acting, the court must notify the court in the adult's home country.

Measures taken by a court in one Member State must be recognised in the others without any special procedure. Recognition can be refused if the adult was not given a genuine and effective chance to be heard, unless there were serious grounds, such as urgency or the adult being unable to express their views. A measure that is enforceable in its home state must be enforced in another state under the same conditions as a domestic measure there.

The regulation also addresses several practical matters. Applicants who received legal aid or cost exemptions in their home state can get the most favourable such benefits in the state where they bring proceedings. Each Member State must designate one or more central authorities to help apply the regulation. Any planned placement of an adult in another Member State must follow a consultation procedure, must take the adult's interests into account, and should reflect their wishes and preferences as far as possible. The state where a measure is carried out can decide how much of the implementation cost the requesting state must pay, but that cost cannot exceed what the measure would cost under the implementing state's own law. Finally, a uniform European Certificate of Support and Representation can be requested by an adult or their representative to show, in another Member State, what matters the representative can act on. Its use is optional, and it is valid for one year.

summary.label: Legislative Observatory, Decision by Parliament, 1st reading
summary.text:
The European Parliament adopted by 531 votes to 93, with 41 abstentions, a legislative resolution on the proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on jurisdiction, applicable law, recognition and enforcement of measures and cooperation in matters relating to the protection of adults.
The European Parliament adopted its position at first reading by amending the proposal as follows:
Scope
This regulation applies in civil matters concerning the protection in cross-border situations of adults who, by reason of an impairment or insufficiency of their personal faculties, are not in a position to protect their interests.
The matters covered may, in particular, include the measures set out in Article 3 of the Hague Convention of 13 January 2000 on the International Protection of Adults (‘the 2000 Hague Convention’), attached to this Regulation, and also: (a) measures to support an adult in exercising his or her legal capacity; (b) powers of representation granted by an adult.
Choice of court
The courts of a Member State other than the one in which an adult is habitually resident will have jurisdiction to take measures where all of the following conditions are met:
(a) the adult chose the courts of that Member State at a time when he or she was in a position to make that choice;
(b) the choice of court was, at the time the choice was made, in favour of a Member State: (i) of which the adult is a national; (ii) of the adult’s habitual residence; (iii) of habitual residence of a person close to the adult prepared to undertake protection of that adult; or (iv) in which property of the adult is located;
(c) the exercise of jurisdiction is not contrary to the interests of the adult;
(d) the courts of a Member State having jurisdiction in accordance with the relevant articles of the 2000 Hague Convention have not exercised their jurisdiction.
The choice must be expressed in writing, dated and signed, or electronically in a way that allows for its durable record. Before taking any action, the court seized must notify the court of the Member State of the adult's habitual residence of its intervention, either directly or through the central authority, using the form in Annex IV.
If the outcome of succession proceedings before a court of a Member State depends on the determination of an incidental question relating to representation of an adult, a court in that Member State may determine that question for the purposes of those proceedings even if that Member State does not have jurisdiction under this regulation.
Law applicable
The amended text clarifies that when the applicable law is that of a State comprising several territorial units, each with their own rules of law in respect of matters governed by this Regulation, the internal conflict-of-law rules of that State will determine the territorial unit whose rules of law are to apply.
Recognition and enforcement of a measure
A measure taken by the courts of a Member State must be recognised in the other Member States without any special procedure being required. The recognition of a measure taken in another Member State may be refused if the measure was taken without the adult having been provided a genuine and effective opportunity to be heard, except where there were serious grounds, taking into account, in particular: (a) the urgency of the case; (b) that the adult was unable to express his or her views.
As regards enforcement , a measure taken in a Member State which is enforceable in that Member State must be enforced in the Member State of enforcement under the same conditions as a measure taken in the Member State of enforcement.
Legal aid
A person applying for legal aid who, in the Member State of origin, has benefitted from complete or partial legal aid or exemption from costs or expenses will be entitled, in any proceedings for recognition or enforcement of a measure, to benefit from the most favourable legal aid or the most extensive exemption from costs or expenses in accordance with the law of the Member State in which proceedings are brought.
Cooperation and communication
Each Member State will designate one or more central authorities to assist it in the application of this regulation and specify the geographical and functional competence of each.
Cooperation in the event of a contemplated investment in another Member State
The contemplated placement of an adult in another Member State must be subject to the procedure set out in Article 33 of the 2000 Hague Convention. The contemplated placement must take into account the interest of the adult and, to the extent possible, the will and preferences of that adult. The court of the requesting Member State must transmit its consultation request to the Central Authority, court or competent authority of the requested Member State using the form set out in Annex VII.
Costs of implementing a measure in another Member State
The national law of the Member State where a measure is to be implemented will determine to what extent the cost of implementation incurred by that Member State is to be borne in the requesting Member State. The cost of implementation will not exceed the costs of the measure under the law of the implementing Member State.
European Certificate of Support and Representation
The Certificate should be a uniform certificate to be intended for use in cross-border situations and issued for use in another Member State. The Certificate may be requested by the adult or the adult’s representative on the basis of an existing measure or confirmed powers of representation. It should therefore only be issued in situations where an adult is not in a position to protect his or her interests and the representative is entitled to actively represent or support that adult in one or more specific matters. The Certificate should include information on the matters in which the representative is entitled to represent or support the adult and on the extent of the powers which the representative is entitled to exercise.
The use of the Certificate should not be mandatory . The Certificate will be valid for a period of one year and set out in an annex to this Regulation.
